## Page framing

- **Hero** `heroBody` — The common types of diabetes, the less common ones, and the clues that your type might be different. Your team decides your type. This chapter helps you ask.
- **Focus** `focus` — The common types: type 1 at any age, type 2, prediabetes, gestational diabetes, and how type 1 starts before symptoms. Less common types: when your type might be different, LADA, MODY, diabetes in babies, genetic syndromes, pancreas conditions and iron overload, cystic fibrosis-related diabetes, and diabetes from medicines or after a transplant.
- **Vibe** `vibe` — Clear and curious: what each type is, and the right questions to ask.
- **Cards intro — eyebrow** `categoriesIntro.eyebrow` — Your type, explained
- **Cards intro — heading** `categoriesIntro.heading` — What your type means
- **Cards intro — body** `categoriesIntro.body` — Most people have one of the common types. Some have a less common type, and for some the type becomes clearer over time. This chapter explains each one, and the clues worth raising with your team. Your team decides your type.

## Cards

### 01 · Type 1, including in adults
Group: **The common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your endocrinologist** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `checkTools` — `meters`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), FreeStyle Lite Meter (4402); `ketones`: Bayer Ketostix (4808); `sensors`: Dexcom G7 Sensor 1-Pack (4227), FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus Sensor (4316)

- Diabetes Canada says 5 to 10% of people with diabetes have type 1. In type 1, the pancreas makes no insulin, so insulin is taken by injection or with a pump ✎ `1.1`
- Type 1 can start in adulthood. Breakthrough T1D estimates that about 71% of people with type 1 in Canada were diagnosed as adults ✎ `1.2`
- Breakthrough T1D also says 85% have no family connection to type 1 `1.3`
- Signs your team looks for include type 1 antibodies in the blood, very little insulin of your own (a low C-peptide), and a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) `1.4`
- Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline names automated insulin delivery as the preferred option for anyone willing and able to use it. Otherwise, it recommends a sensor (CGM) with a pump or with injections `1.5`

> **Note** `1.note` — Ketones and DKA are covered in Staying Safe. The test names are explained in Could my type be different?

### 02 · Type 2
Group: **The common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your doctor** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `meterAndStrips` — `oneTouch`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), OneTouch Verio Test Strips (4948); `contour`: Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Contour Next Test Strips (4714)

*Carries an emergency or same-day line: rendered open, never collapsed, and every figure on it renders in both locales.*

- Type 2 is the most common type. Diabetes Canada says 90 to 95% of people with diabetes have it `2.1`
- Risk factors include being over 40, having diabetes in your family, and your ethnic background. Type 2 may cause no symptoms `2.2`
- Diabetes Canada diagnoses diabetes with any one of these results: `2.3`
- A fasting blood sugar of 7.0 mmol/L or higher `2.4`
- An A1C of 6.5% or higher, in adults. It isn’t used when type 1 is suspected `2.5`
- A blood sugar of 11.1 mmol/L or higher, 2 hours after a glucose drink or at any time of day `2.6`
- Without symptoms, a second test on another day confirms it `2.7`
- With symptoms of high blood sugar, Diabetes Canada says the diagnosis is made without a second test, and treatment shouldn’t be delayed. Contact your doctor or another health-care provider today, without waiting for a second test. Emergency signs are in Staying Safe ✎ `2.8`
- For children and teens with type 2, Diabetes Canada says antibody testing should be considered, because up to 10 to 20% test positive `2.9`

> **Note** `2.note` — If your diabetes doesn’t fit the usual picture, see Could my type be different?

*Sources for this card:* Type 2 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); Definition, Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes, Prediabetes and Metabolic Syndrome (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Type 2 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Hyperglycemia (Diabetes Canada)

### 03 · Prediabetes
Group: **The common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your doctor** · Products shown: *none*

- Prediabetes means a blood sugar above the usual range, but below the numbers for diabetes. Diabetes Canada uses any one of these results: `3.1`
- A fasting blood sugar of 6.1 to 6.9 mmol/L `3.2`
- An A1C of 6.0 to 6.4% `3.3`
- A blood sugar of 7.8 to 11.0 mmol/L, 2 hours after a glucose drink `3.4`
- Diabetes Canada’s Prediabetes page links to the CANRISK test `3.5`
- Not everyone with prediabetes goes on to develop type 2, but Diabetes Canada says many people do `3.6`

> **Note** `3.note` — Ask your doctor what your numbers mean for you, and when to test again.

*Sources for this card:* Definition, Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes, Prediabetes and Metabolic Syndrome (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Prediabetes (Diabetes Canada)

### 04 · Gestational, or diabetes from before pregnancy?
Group: **The common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `meterAndStrips` — `oneTouch`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), OneTouch Verio Test Strips (4948); `contour`: Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Contour Next Test Strips (4714)

- Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found during pregnancy. Diabetes from before pregnancy, type 1 or type 2, was diagnosed before you conceived `4.1`
- Diabetes that is clearly there early in pregnancy is counted on its own, as overt diabetes, not as gestational diabetes `4.2`
- If you’re at high risk, Diabetes Canada’s guideline includes an A1C test before 20 weeks `4.3`
- Screening for gestational diabetes is offered between 24 and 28 weeks `4.4`
- Diabetes Canada says gestational diabetes affects 3 to 20% of pregnancies and usually goes away after birth. It raises the chance of type 2 and heart disease later `4.5`
- After the birth, Diabetes Canada recommends a glucose tolerance test between 6 weeks and 6 months `4.6`
- International guidance from the University of Exeter says a steady fasting blood sugar of 5.5 to 8 mmol/L, with diabetes in the family, can point to a single-gene type called GCK-MODY. If that sounds like you, tell your team early in pregnancy `4.7`

> **Note** `4.note` — Fill in the reminder with your team before the birth. Pregnancy with type 1 or type 2 is covered in This Might Be You.

*Sources for this card:* Diabetes and Pregnancy (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Glucose testing – screening for gestational diabetes (Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada (Pregnancy Info)); Gestational Diabetes (Diabetes Canada); GCK Guidelines in Pregnancy (University of Exeter, diabetesgenes.org (UK))

### 05 · Type 1 starts before symptoms
Group: **The common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your doctor** · Products shown: *none*

- Type 1 starts before there are symptoms. Breakthrough T1D describes stages 1 and 2 coming before diagnosis, and international guidance defines the stages like this: `5.1`
- Stage 1: two or more type 1 antibodies, with normal blood sugar `5.2`
- Stage 2: two or more type 1 antibodies, with blood sugar starting to rise above normal ✎ `5.3`
- Stage 3: type 1 diabetes is diagnosed `5.4`
- Breakthrough T1D says two or more antibodies that last over time mean a high risk of type 1. Only 10 to 15% of people newly diagnosed have a family history `5.5`
- TrialNet screens relatives of people with type 1 at no cost, with a home finger-stick kit or a lab visit, anywhere in Canada. Immediate relatives aged 2 to 45 and other relatives aged 2 to 20 can take part. Results take 4 to 6 weeks `5.6`
- Breakthrough T1D also lists FEDERATE-Can, in Quebec. CanScreen, a Canadian research program on screening newborns and children, says it is launching in fall 2026 or winter 2027 `5.7`
- Diabetes Canada’s 2025 type 1 guideline makes no recommendation about screening `5.8`
- People who test positive are followed over time. International guidance says they should be taught, and reminded, about the signs of diabetes and DKA `5.9`
- In May 2025, Health Canada approved teplizumab (Tzield) for people aged 8 and older in stage 2, to delay stage 3. Canada’s Drug Agency says that in one study it delayed stage 3 by about 2 years, and that it can cause side effects, including serious ones. The agency recommended that public drug plans not cover it, and Diabetes Canada says it isn’t on any provincial or territorial drug plan. It’s available out of pocket, through private insurance, or through compassionate access ✎ `5.10`
- Breakthrough T1D also says you can ask your doctor to look at UncoverT1D, a website run by Sanofi, the company that makes teplizumab, that has information for health care providers about which tests to order `5.11`

> **Note** `5.note` — Whether to screen, and what a result means, is a conversation with your doctor. A screening result isn’t a diagnosis.

*Sources for this card:* Stages and diagnosis of T1D (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); 2026 ADA Diabetes Standards of Medical Care Clinical Guideline Summary (American Diabetes Association (US), via a Guideline Central summary); Consensus guidance for monitoring individuals with islet autoantibody-positive pre-stage 3 type 1 diabetes (Diabetologia 2024 (also Diabetes Care); Phillip et al., international consensus); TrialNet (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); CanScreen T1D Research Consortium (CanScreen T1D Research Consortium (funded by Breakthrough T1D and CIHR)); Glycemic Management Across the Lifespan for People With Type 1 Diabetes (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Access to T1D immunotherapy drug Tzield in Canada (Diabetes Canada); Tzield update (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); TZIELD Product Monograph Including Patient Medication Information (sanofi-aventis Canada Inc. / Health Canada Drug Product Database); Reimbursement Recommendation: Teplizumab (Tzield) (Canada’s Drug Agency (CDA-AMC))

### 06 · Could my type be different?
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown: *none*

**Why the type matters** `6.s1`

- Your diabetes team decides your type. Diabetes Canada says some cases are difficult to classify `6.s1.1`
- An international consensus from the American Diabetes Association and the European Association for the Study of Diabetes found that more than 40% of people who develop type 1 after age 30 are first treated as type 2 `6.s1.2`
- Diabetes Canada says the right type may change your treatment. International guidance adds that it can show whether your family might be offered testing `6.s1.3`

**Clues to mention to your team** `6.s2`

- You were diagnosed at a younger age, or you have a lower body weight ✎ `6.s2.1`
- You lost weight without trying, or you’ve had ketones or DKA `6.s2.2`
- You needed insulin within 1 to 2 years of diagnosis `6.s2.3`
- Diabetes runs through generations of your family, such as a parent and a grandparent `6.s2.4`
- You were diagnosed before 6 months of age `6.s2.5`
- You have hearing loss, and there’s diabetes on your mother’s side of the family. International guidance links the two `6.s2.6`
- You’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, or you have cystic fibrosis or iron overload (hemochromatosis) `6.s2.7`
- Your diabetes started after a transplant, or after you began steroids, an antipsychotic, an anti-rejection medicine or cancer immunotherapy `6.s2.8`
- You have a hormone condition, such as Cushing’s syndrome or acromegaly `6.s2.9`

**Tests that can help** `6.s3`

- Antibody tests look for signs of type 1. International guidance suggests testing for GAD antibodies first `6.s3.1`
- A C-peptide test shows how much insulin your body still makes. It’s most useful months to years after diagnosis, and not during a very high blood sugar `6.s3.2`
- Genetic tests look for single-gene types, such as MODY. A specialist usually arranges them `6.s3.3`
- Diabetes Canada says antibody levels fade over time, and the tests aren’t accurate enough to use for everyone. When your type is hard to tell, a positive test points to type 1, but a negative test doesn’t rule type 1 out. Your team decides ✎ `6.s3.4`

**Getting tested in Canada** `6.s4`

- Your doctor or specialist orders these tests. In Manitoba, for example, the GAD antibody test is ordered by endocrinologists, and other doctors need an approval form `6.s4.1`
- What’s covered varies by province. In BC, for example, the antibody tests aren’t covered by MSP `6.s4.2`
- Genetic testing usually needs a referral. A test that isn’t offered in your province may need approval before it’s sent elsewhere `6.s4.3`

> **Note** `6.note` — Not a diagnostic tool. These clues are things to mention, not signs that your type is wrong. Your team decides what to test. Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Definition, Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes, Prediabetes and Metabolic Syndrome (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Type 2 Diabetes in Children and Adolescents (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); The management of type 1 diabetes in adults (ADA/EASD consensus report, 2021) (American Diabetes Association and European Association for the Study of Diabetes; Holt et al., Diabetologia 2021); What is MODY? (University of Exeter, diabetesgenes.org (UK)); Maturity onset diabetes of the young (MODY) (Diabetes UK); Maternally Inherited Diabetes and Deafness (MIDD) (University of Exeter, diabetesgenes.org (UK)); Etiologic Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); 2026 ADA Diabetes Standards of Medical Care Clinical Guideline Summary (American Diabetes Association (US), via a Guideline Central summary); Diabetes and Transplantation (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); C-peptide and islet autoantibody testing (University of Exeter, diabetesgenes.org (UK)); ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: The diagnosis and management of monogenic diabetes in children and adolescents (International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD); Greeley et al., Pediatric Diabetes 2022); Genetics clinic directory (Ontario Health) (Ontario Health); Anti-GAD65 (St. Boniface Hospital laboratory manual) (St. Boniface Hospital laboratory manual (Manitoba)); Type 1 diabetes auto-antibody testing (BCDiabetes handout) (BCDiabetes (clinic handout)); Application for Prior Approval for Full Payment of Insured OOC & OOP Laboratory & Genetics Testing (014-4521-84) (Government of Ontario (Ministry of Health)); Out-of-Province & Out-of-Country Laboratory or Genetic Test Funding Request (Provincial Health Services Authority (BC), Provincial Laboratory Medicine Services); Tests génétiques non disponibles au Québec (CHU Sainte-Justine)

### 07 · LADA: type 1 that starts slowly in adults
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your endocrinologist** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `checkTools` — `meters`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), FreeStyle Lite Meter (4402); `ketones`: Bayer Ketostix (4808); `sensors`: Dexcom G7 Sensor 1-Pack (4227), FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus Sensor (4316)

- **Badge** `7.badge` — International guidance
- LADA (latent autoimmune diabetes in adults) is a slow-starting form of type 1. It’s sometimes called type 1.5 `7.1`
- The usual pattern: it starts after age 30, antibodies are present, and insulin isn’t needed for at least the first 6 months `7.2`
- It’s often first diagnosed and managed as type 2 `7.3`
- An antibody test, usually GAD, confirms it. International guidance says a C-peptide test helps guide treatment `7.4`
- Most people need insulin sooner than with type 2, and the timing varies widely. International guidance says it tends to come sooner with higher antibody levels, or more than one antibody `7.5`
- Breakthrough T1D describes a modified type 1 plan, which can include some type 2 medicines. International guidance says others are less suitable, so ask your team before any change `7.6`
- Estimates of how common it is range from 2 to 12% of adult diabetes (an international consensus) to about 10% (Breakthrough T1D) `7.7`

> **Note** `7.note` — Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. Bring these questions to your team. The signs of lows and ketones are in Staying Safe. ✎ *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Management of Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults: A Consensus Statement From an International Expert Panel (Diabetes (ADA journal); Buzzetti et al., an international expert panel); Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA) (Diabetes UK); Definition, Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes, Prediabetes and Metabolic Syndrome (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines)

### 08 · MODY: single-gene diabetes
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your endocrinologist** · Products shown: *none*

- **Badge** `8.badge` — International guidance
- MODY is caused by a change in a single gene. Diabetes Canada calls single-gene diabetes rare. International estimates range from 1 to 2% of diabetes for MODY (Diabetes UK, University of Exeter) to 1 to 5% for all single-gene types (the US NIDDK) ✎ `8.1`
- Diabetes UK says about 9 in 10 people with MODY are first told they have another type `8.2`
- Clues include being diagnosed young, not having obesity, having no type 1 antibodies, and a parent with diabetes, in two or more generations ✎ `8.3`
- How young varies. Diabetes Canada and Diabetes UK use under 25. Other international guidance uses under 30, or 35 and under. Your team decides `8.4`
- It’s confirmed with a genetic test, usually after antibody and C-peptide tests `8.5`
- GCK: a mild, steady high blood sugar that usually needs no treatment `8.6`
- HNF1A and HNF4A: often treated with tablets rather than insulin. A specialist decides `8.7`
- HNF1B: can affect the kidneys, with cysts, and other organs. It’s usually treated with insulin `8.8`
- Each child of a parent with MODY has a 50% chance of inheriting it. Once the family’s gene change is known, relatives can be tested, and genetic counselling can help `8.9`
- In pregnancy with GCK, care depends on whether the baby inherited it, so tell your team early. HNF4A can mean a larger baby, and low blood sugar in the newborn `8.10`
- In a Canadian study of children with single-gene diabetes, GCK was the most common type: 19 of 29 children `8.11`
- Most of the evidence comes from people of European ancestry. The usual clues are less reliable for people of other ancestries `8.12`

> **Note** `8.note` — Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change is made with your specialist. Fill in the family tree before your appointment. It helps your team, or a genetic counsellor, see the pattern. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Maturity onset diabetes of the young (MODY) (Diabetes UK); What is MODY? ### 09 · Diabetes in babies
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your endocrinologist** · Products shown: *none*

- **Badge** `9.badge` — International guidance
- Diabetes diagnosed before 6 months of age is usually caused by a single gene `9.1`
- Diabetes Canada says every baby diagnosed before 6 months should have genetic testing `9.2`
- The University of Exeter says it affects about 1 in 100,000 births. The US NIDDK says about 1 in 90,000, and describes it in the first 6 to 12 months `9.3`
- Some forms are temporary, and others are lifelong `9.4`
- The genetic result matters. For the potassium-channel types, international guidance says about 9 in 10 people can switch from insulin to tablets under specialist care, with more benefit the earlier it happens `9.5`
- Adults told they have type 1 who were diagnosed before 6 months should have their diagnosis reviewed `9.6`

> **Note** `9.note` — Don’t stop or lower insulin because of anything on this page. Any change in treatment is planned with a specialist team. *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

*Sources for this card:* Definition, Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes, Prediabetes and Metabolic Syndrome (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); About Neonatal Diabetes (University of Exeter, diabetesgenes.org (UK)); Monogenic Diabetes (MODY & Neonatal Diabetes Mellitus) (National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (US)); ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: The diagnosis and management of monogenic diabetes in children and adolescents (International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD); Greeley et al., Pediatric Diabetes 2022); Treatment of KCNJ11 and ABCC8 permanent neonatal diabetes with sulphonylureas (University of Exeter, diabetesgenes.org (UK))

### 10 · Genetic syndromes with diabetes
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your endocrinologist** · Products shown: *none*

- **Badge** `10.badge` — International guidance
- Some single-gene types come with other health signs, such as hearing loss or vision loss `10.1`
- MIDD (maternally inherited diabetes and deafness) passes from a mother to all her children, though how much it affects each child varies. Fathers don’t pass it on `10.2`
- Diabetes starts at 37 on average, and insulin is usually needed within about 2 years `10.3`
- Hearing loss is common and often comes first. The heart, kidneys, eyes and gut can be affected too `10.4`
- A urine sample is preferred for the test `10.5`
- Wolfram syndrome is very rare, about 1 in 500,000 people, and both parents carry the gene. Diabetes usually starts around age 6, and vision loss from the optic nerve around age 11 `10.6`
- Lipodystrophy affects where the body stores fat. Clues include little or unusually placed body fat, high triglycerides (a blood fat), and darkened skin in body folds `10.7`
- These are confirmed with genetic testing, arranged through a specialist `10.8`

> **Note** `10.note` — If several of these sound familiar, ask your team whether a genetics referral would help.

*Sources for this card:* ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: The diagnosis and management of monogenic diabetes in children and adolescents (International Society for Pediatric and Adolescent Diabetes (ISPAD); Greeley et al., Pediatric Diabetes 2022); Maternally Inherited Diabetes and Deafness (MIDD) (University of Exeter, diabetesgenes.org (UK)); Wolfram syndrome (MedlinePlus Genetics (US National Library of Medicine))

### 11 · Pancreas conditions and iron overload
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your diabetes team** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `checkTools` — `meters`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), FreeStyle Lite Meter (4402); `ketones`: Bayer Ketostix (4808); `sensors`: Dexcom G7 Sensor 1-Pack (4227), FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus Sensor (4316)

- Diabetes Canada lists diseases of the pancreas as a cause of diabetes, including pancreatitis, surgery or injury to the pancreas, a growth in the pancreas, and cystic fibrosis `11.1`
- Hemochromatosis, where the body stores too much iron, is on the same list. The Canadian Hemochromatosis Society says it can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes `11.2`
- About 1 in 300 Canadians have two copies of the gene change that puts them at risk. BC’s guideline says fewer than 1 in 10 of them develop the disease `11.3`
- An iron test isn’t part of a standard blood test, so it has to be asked for. A genetic test confirms hemochromatosis `11.4`
- Close family, such as parents, brothers, sisters and children, should be tested `11.5`
- Treatment removes blood regularly (phlebotomy). The society says it can mildly improve diabetes `11.6`

> **Note** `11.note` — If you’ve had pancreas disease or surgery, ask your team what it means for your diabetes care. Lows and ketones are covered in Staying Safe.

*Sources for this card:* Etiologic Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); The Condition (Canadian Hemochromatosis Society) (Canadian Hemochromatosis Society); FAQ (Canadian Hemochromatosis Society) (Canadian Hemochromatosis Society); High Ferritin and Iron Overload (BC Guidelines) (Government of British Columbia (BC Guidelines)); Treatment & Maintenance (Canadian Hemochromatosis Society) (Canadian Hemochromatosis Society)

### 12 · Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your CF clinic** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `checkTools` — `meters`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), FreeStyle Lite Meter (4402); `ketones`: Bayer Ketostix (4808); `sensors`: Dexcom G7 Sensor 1-Pack (4227), FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus Sensor (4316)

- Cystic fibrosis can affect the pancreas and lead to diabetes, called cystic fibrosis-related diabetes (CFRD) `12.1`
- It becomes more common with age. In Canada, 3.6% of people with CF under 18 have it, rising to 58.7% of adults over 35 `12.2`
- Screening is yearly from age 10, through your CF clinic. Cystic Fibrosis Canada’s guideline starts with an A1C test and adds a glucose tolerance test when needed. The glucose tolerance test may be used first if A1C isn’t reliable for you. Your clinic decides ✎ `12.3`
- Insulin is the main treatment, and the only medicine used for children. Cystic Fibrosis Canada says some adults may have other options `12.4`
- If you use insulin, ask your team for a plan for lows. Cystic Fibrosis Canada’s guideline says people on insulin, and their families or carers, should be taught how to use glucagon. International guidance adds that the body’s own response to a low is weaker in CF ✎ `12.5`
- In pregnancy, if you don’t already have CFRD, a glucose tolerance test is done early, at 12 to 16 weeks or when the pregnancy is confirmed. If that one is normal, it’s repeated at 24 to 28 weeks `12.6`
- After a transplant, 25 to 50% of people with CF who didn’t have CFRD before develop diabetes `12.7`
- Yearly eye, kidney and nerve checks start 5 years after diagnosis `12.8`
- Your CF clinic works with a diabetes team, ideally including a diabetes educator `12.9`

> **Note** `12.note` — Glucagon and the Rule of 15 are in Staying Safe.

*Sources for this card:* Etiologic Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Cystic Fibrosis Related Diabetes (CFRD): A First Canadian Clinical Practice Guideline — Guidelines & Standards of Care (Cystic Fibrosis Canada) (Cystic Fibrosis Canada); ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus Guidelines 2022: Management of cystic fibrosis-related diabetes in children and adolescents (ISPAD; Ode et al., Pediatric Diabetes 2022)

### 13 · From medicines, or after a transplant
Group: **Less common types** · Referral chip: **Ask your prescriber** · Products shown (shop strip after the referral chip; each only while the store shows it, sells it and has it in stock, and never one whose description names or links another retailer): `checkTools` — `meters`: OneTouch Verio Reflect Meter (4287), Contour NEXT ONE Meter (4524), Accu-Chek Guide Meter (4556), FreeStyle Lite Meter (4402); `ketones`: Bayer Ketostix (4808); `sensors`: Dexcom G7 Sensor 1-Pack (4227), FreeStyle Libre 3 Plus Sensor (4316)

- Diabetes Canada lists some medicines that can cause diabetes, including steroids, some antipsychotics and some anti-rejection medicines `13.1`
- Diabetes Canada’s hospital guideline says 20 to 50% of people without diabetes who take steroids develop high blood sugar. Checking blood sugar for 48 hours after starting may be considered `13.2`
- Some antipsychotic medicines can cause weight gain and raise blood sugar and cholesterol `13.3`
- In children and teens, the risk of type 2 diabetes is 2 to 3 times higher, and the rise can show within the first year `13.4`
- Diabetes Canada recommends checking weight, blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol before you start, then on a schedule that differs for each check. Ask your prescriber when yours are due `13.5`
- International guidance from the American Diabetes Association says to check blood sugar before you start a checkpoint inhibitor, a type of cancer immunotherapy, and at every visit while you’re on it. An international consensus says this diabetes can come on with DKA `13.6`
- After a transplant, the risk depends on things like the steroid dose, some infections, and which anti-rejection medicine is used `13.7`
- Diabetes Canada’s guideline checks blood sugar before the transplant, in the first 3 months after it, and with an A1C at 3 and 12 months, then every year. It says a glucose tolerance test is more sensitive than A1C, and it’s used if A1C isn’t reliable. Your team decides ✎ `13.8`
- An international consensus says 20 to 40% of people who have a heart, lung or liver transplant develop diabetes `13.9`
- Know the signs of high blood sugar and ketones. They’re in Staying Safe `13.10`

> **Note** `13.note` — Don’t stop or change how you take any of these medicines on your own, even if your blood sugar goes up. Ask your prescriber or pharmacist first. ✎ *(kept outside the collapsed part of the card)*

(expert opinion, no GRADE))

## Referral band

*Sources for the band:* Anti-GAD65 (St. Boniface Hospital laboratory manual) (St. Boniface Hospital laboratory manual (Manitoba)); Type 1 diabetes auto-antibody testing (BCDiabetes handout) (BCDiabetes (clinic handout)); Definition, Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes, Prediabetes and Metabolic Syndrome (Diabetes Canada, Clinical Practice Guidelines); Genetics clinic directory (Ontario Health) (Ontario Health); Application for Prior Approval for Full Payment of Insured OOC & OOP Laboratory & Genetics Testing (014-4521-84) (Government of Ontario (Ministry of Health)); Out-of-Province & Out-of-Country Laboratory or Genetic Test Funding Request (Provincial Health Services Authority (BC), Provincial Laboratory Medicine Services); Tests génétiques non disponibles au Québec (CHU Sainte-Justine); TrialNet (Breakthrough T1D Canada (formerly JDRF)); Cystic Fibrosis Related Diabetes (CFRD): A First Canadian Clinical Practice Guideline — Guidelines & Standards of Care (Cystic Fibrosis Canada) (Cystic Fibrosis Canada)

**Who does the testing** `band.heading`

- **Your doctor or specialist** `band.1` — Orders antibody, C-peptide and A1C tests. Some labs limit antibody tests to specialists unless an approval form is sent. Bring your clues: see Could my type be different?
  - *Where card 6's title appears in this body, it links to card 6.*
- **A genetics clinic** `band.2` — Single-gene testing usually needs a referral. A test not offered in your province may need approval first. See MODY: single-gene diabetes.
  - *Where card 8's title appears in this body, it links to card 8.*
- **TrialNet, for relatives** `band.3` — Free type 1 antibody screening for relatives, at home or at a lab, anywhere in Canada. See Type 1 starts before symptoms.
  - *Where card 5's title appears in this body, it links to card 5.*
- **Your CF clinic** `band.4` — Yearly diabetes screening from age 10 for people with cystic fibrosis. See Cystic fibrosis-related diabetes.
  - *Where card 12's title appears in this body, it links to card 12.*

## Closing

**Knowing your type** `closing.heading`

Your type shapes your care, and it can be looked at again if something doesn’t fit. Bring your clues and your questions to your team. `closing.body`

## Disclaimer

This is general information, not medical advice, and it is not a diagnosis. Your diabetes team decides your type, which tests you need, and your treatment. `disclaimer`

*Released by the source check, and now in the copy: prediabetes and the chance of type 2 (3.6); A1C as the average over the past 2 to 3 months (6.fig.terms.4); insulin "within 1 to 2 years" from CPG Ch3 (6.s2.3, and the family tree’s column); teplizumab from age 8, in stage 2 (5.10); checkpoint-inhibitor diabetes coming on with DKA (13.6). Released by the clinical rulings of 2026-10-06: teplizumab’s "about 2 years" delay, beside its serious side effects (5.10, C26); Breakthrough T1D’s UncoverT1D pointer (5.11, C36). No card is held whole: card 11 keeps six sourced items without the type 3c detail.*
